_note: One sentence on the name, keyed by Lucas's epithet (lowercase) or by specimen id. Only names whose referent is unambiguous are included. Linnaeus and his followers named the great swallowtails after Trojan and Greek heroes, the whites and yellows after nymphs and heroines, and later authors honoured naturalists.
priamus: Named by Linnaeus for Priam, king of Troy. In his 1758 system the largest swallowtails were the Trojans, the Equites Trojani, and their names still ring of the Iliad.
rhadamantus: Named for Rhadamanthus, the Cretan lawgiver who became a judge of the dead. Boisduval gave the name in 1836; Lucas printed it the year the species was described.
ulysses: Named by Linnaeus for Ulysses, the wanderer of the Odyssey. The name has never changed, which is rare for a butterfly described in 1758.
hector: Named for Hector, Troy's champion. A Trojan name from Linnaeus, given to a red-bodied swallowtail he placed among the Trojans.
sarpedon: Named for Sarpedon, the Lycian king killed by Patroclus before the walls of Troy.
coon: Not a hero at all: Fabricius took the name from Coön, a Trojan warrior in the Iliad who wounded Agamemnon.
vertumnus: Named for Vertumnus, the Roman god of the changing seasons and of gardens.
philenor: The name means lover of husband in Greek; Linnaeus gave it in 1771 to the pipevine swallowtail of North America.
demoleus: Named for Demoleus, a Greek slain by Aeneas in the Aeneid. Linnaeus placed the species among the Achivi, the Greek knights.
deiphobus: Named for Deiphobus, son of Priam, who took Helen as his wife after Paris fell.
polymnestor: Named for Polymnestor, the Thracian king of Euripides' Hecuba, who murdered Priam's youngest son for his gold.
helenus: Named for Helenus, the seer-prince of Troy and twin of Cassandra.
cresphontes: Named for Cresphontes, a descendant of Heracles who won Messenia by lot when the Peloponnese was divided.
brutus: Named for Brutus, the Roman who drove out the Tarquin kings. Fabricius named it in 1793.
dardanus: Named for Dardanus, the mythical founder of the Trojan line, from whom the Dardanelles take their name.
aeneas: Named by Linnaeus for Aeneas, the Trojan prince who escaped the burning city to found the Roman line.
sesostris: Named for Sesostris, the legendary Egyptian conqueror of Herodotus, who is usually identified with the pharaohs Senusret.
ascanius: Named for Ascanius, son of Aeneas, who founded Alba Longa.
belus: Named for Belus, the legendary king of Egypt or Tyre and father of Dido in the Aeneid.
polydamas: Named by Linnaeus for Polydamas, the Trojan counsellor and friend of Hector who urged caution the night before the Greeks broke out.
turnus: Named for Turnus, king of the Rutuli and Aeneas's rival in the Aeneid. The species is now Papilio glaucus, the tiger swallowtail.
xuthus: Named by Linnaeus for Xuthus, a son of Hellen and ancestor of the Ionians.
troilus: Named by Linnaeus for Troilus, the young prince of Troy slain by Achilles.
asterias: Asterias means starry; Fabricius's name for the black swallowtail, whose rows of yellow spots the engraver has picked out here.
protesilaus: Named by Linnaeus for Protesilaus, the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy and the first to die there.
polixenus: Named for Polyxena, Priam's daughter, sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles.
macareus: Named for Macareus, a name borne by several figures of Greek myth, among them a son of Aeolus.
zenobius: Named for Zenobia, the third-century queen of Palmyra who defied Rome.
cynortas: Named for Cynortas, a mythical king of Sparta.
poppea: Named for Poppaea Sabina, the wife of Nero.
paulina: Named for Paulina, a Roman matron's name; Cramer and Fabricius favoured such names for the tropical whites.
calypso: Named for Calypso, the nymph who kept Odysseus on her island for seven years.
teutonia: Named for the Teutons; Fabricius often reached for tribal and place names when the classical stock ran thin.
judith: Named for Judith, the biblical heroine who beheaded the Assyrian general Holofernes.
belisama: Named for Belisama, a Celtic goddess equated by the Romans with Minerva.
philyra: Named for Philyra, the Oceanid who was mother of the centaur Chiron.
hyparete: Named for Hipparete, the wife of the Athenian statesman Alcibiades.
harpalice: Named for Harpalyce, the Thracian huntress raised by her father to fight as a warrior.
aganippe: Named for Aganippe, the spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses.
pyrrha: Named for Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion, who with him repeopled the earth after the flood by throwing stones over their shoulders.
argia: Named for Argia, daughter of Adrastus and wife of Polynices in the tale of Thebes.
valeria: Named for the Valerii, one of the great patrician families of Rome.
nina: Nina is a girl's name, not a myth; Fabricius gave it to this little white in 1793.
leucippe: Named for Leucippe, a name of several heroines meaning white horse.
glaucippe: Glaucippe means grey-green horse in Greek, a companion name to Leucippe given by Linnaeus in 1758.
marianne: Named for Marianne; Cramer used the names of women of his own day as freely as those of antiquity.
pirene: Named for Pirene, the fountain of Corinth where Pegasus was said to drink.
venilia: Named for Venilia, a Roman sea nymph, wife of Janus in some accounts.
fausta: Fausta means fortunate in Latin, and was the name of Constantine's empress.
danae: Named for Danaë, mother of Perseus, to whom Zeus came as a shower of gold.
evippe: Named for Euippe, one of the Danaids.
ione: Named for Ione, a sea nymph, one of the Nereids.
hecabe: Named for Hecuba, queen of Troy and mother of Hector. Linnaeus gave the name in 1758 to this common yellow of the East.
candida: Candida means shining white in Latin, a curious name for a yellow butterfly; it refers to the white of the underside.
nicippe: Named for Nicippe, a daughter of Pelops.
elathea: Named for Elatea, an ancient town of Phocis in central Greece.
amata: Named for Amata, queen of the Latins and mother of Lavinia in the Aeneid.
philodice: Named for Philodice, a Naiad, wife of Leucippus.
caesonia: Named for Caesonia, the last wife of the emperor Caligula.
scylla: Named for Scylla, the sea monster of the Strait of Messina in the Odyssey.
evadne: Named for Evadne, who threw herself on her husband Capaneus's funeral pyre at Thebes.
argante: Named for Argante, an Amazon queen in Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered.
trite: Named by Linnaeus in 1758 for Trite, a name of Athena.
philea: Philea means loving in Greek; Linnaeus's name for this orange-barred sulphur.
clorinde: Named for Clorinda, the warrior maiden of Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered, killed unknowingly by the knight who loved her.
leachiana: Named for William Elford Leach, zoologist at the British Museum, who died in 1836, the year this book was completed.
marsyas: Named for Marsyas, the satyr who challenged Apollo to a music contest and was flayed for losing.
narbal: Named for Narbal, the Tyrian admiral in Fénelon's Télémaque, a favourite book of the eighteenth century.
plexippe: Named for Plexippus, uncle of Meleager, killed by him after the Calydonian boar hunt. The Monarch has carried the name since 1758.
hegesippe: Named for Hegesippus, the Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes' enemies.
cleone: Named for Cleone, a nymph, daughter of the river Asopus.
sara: Sara is a plain Hebrew name; Fabricius gave it to this small longwing in 1793.
melpomene: Named by Linnaeus for Melpomene, the Muse of tragedy.
phillis: Named for Phyllis, the Thracian princess who hanged herself waiting for Demophon and became an almond tree.
charitonia: Named by Linnaeus for the Charites, the Graces of Greek myth.
ilione: Named for Ilione, eldest daughter of Priam.
thalia: Named by Linnaeus for Thalia, the Muse of comedy and one of the Graces.
vibilia: Named for Vibilia, the Roman goddess of journeys and of travellers who had lost their way.
julia: Named by Fabricius for the Julian house of Rome. The modern spelling, Dryas iulia, keeps the Latin i.
juno: Named for Juno, queen of the Roman gods.
eva: Named for Eve, the first woman.
humboldtii: Named for Alexander von Humboldt, whose travels in the Americas with Bonpland filled the cabinets of Paris.
dido: Named for Dido, queen of Carthage, who loved and lost Aeneas. Linnaeus gave the name in 1767.
lamarckii: Named for Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, who coined the word invertebrate and whose lectures shaped Lucas's generation of naturalists.
leschenault: Named for Jean-Baptiste Leschenault de la Tour, botanist of the Baudin expedition, who collected in Java.
penthesilea: Named for Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, killed by Achilles at Troy.
cydippe: Named for Cydippe, the Athenian girl tricked into marriage by an apple inscribed with a vow, in a tale told by Callimachus.
idalia: Idalia is an epithet of Venus, from Idalium in Cyprus where she was worshipped.
juliana: Named for Juliana, a Roman feminine of the Julian name.
amathea: Named for Amathea, one of the Nereids.
charonia: Named for Charon, the ferryman of the dead.
sophronia: Sophronia means prudent in Greek, and is the name of the Christian maiden in Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered.
orithya: Named by Linnaeus for Orithyia, an Amazon queen.
clelia: Named for Cloelia, the Roman girl who escaped Etruscan captivity by swimming the Tiber.
oenone: Named for Oenone, the nymph who was Paris's first love and who refused to heal him when he lay dying.
cuvierii: Named for Georges Cuvier, the great anatomist of the Paris museum where Lucas worked; he died in 1832.
pollux: Named for Pollux, the immortal twin of Castor; Cramer had already called the same butterfly Castor.
tiridates: Named for Tiridates, the name of several kings of Parthia and Armenia.
nisus: Named for Nisus, king of Megara, whose purple lock of hair held the fate of his city.
pyrrhus: Named by Linnaeus for Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, whose costly victories gave us the phrase Pyrrhic victory.
clytemnestra: Named for Clytemnestra, who murdered her husband Agamemnon on his return from Troy.
decius: Named for Decius Mus, the Roman consul who rode into the enemy line to die for his army.
veranes: Named for Veranes, a Persian prince mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus.
orion: Named for Orion, the giant hunter placed among the stars.
rogerii: Named for a M. Roger, the collector who supplied the Cuban specimen; Godart honoured many such correspondents.
steneles: Named by Linnaeus for Sthenelus, charioteer of Diomedes at Troy.
laurentia: Named for Laurentia, wife of the shepherd who raised Romulus and Remus.
gelania: Named for Gelanor, an early king of Argos.
sangaris: Named for the river Sangarius in Phrygia, now the Sakarya in Turkey.
amasia: Named for Amasia, the ancient city of Pontus, birthplace of the geographer Strabo.
callisto: Named for Callisto, the nymph turned into a bear and then into the Great Bear.
alimena: Named for Alcmene, mother of Heracles; Linnaeus spelt it Alimena.
salmasis: Named for Salmacis, the nymph who merged with Hermaphroditus in her pool.
clymenus: Named for Clymenus, a name of several figures in myth, among them a king of Orchomenus.
demophon: Named by Linnaeus for Demophon, son of Theseus and king of Athens.
demodice: Named for Demodice, a figure of the tale of Phrixus and the golden ram.
inachis: Named for Inachus, the river god and first king of Argos.
leonte: Named for Leontes, a king of Sicily in Shakespeare's Winter's Tale, or for the Greek name meaning lion-like.
menelaus: Named by Linnaeus for Menelaus, king of Sparta and husband of Helen. He named the female Nestor, after the old counsellor of the Greeks.
laertes: Named for Laertes, father of Odysseus.
lycaon: Named for Lycaon, the Arcadian king turned into a wolf by Zeus.
sophorae: Named for the plant, Sophora, on which Linnaeus believed the caterpillar fed. It actually feeds on palms.
toxea: Named for Toxeus, a brother of Meleager killed at the Calydonian boar hunt.
nicaeus: Named for Nicaea, the city in Bithynia where the Christian creed was fixed in AD 325.
lena: Named by Linnaeus in 1767; Lena is a plain girl's name, unusual among his classical choices.
nereis: Named for the Nereids, the fifty sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus.
versicolor: Versicolor simply means of changing colours in Latin.
polycaon: Named for Polycaon, a Spartan prince who became the first king of Messenia.
agavus: Named for Agave, daughter of Cadmus, who in her frenzy tore her own son Pentheus apart.
bathycles: Named for Bathycles of Magnesia, the sculptor who made the throne of Apollo at Amyclae.
evander: Named for Evander, the Arcadian who settled on the Palatine before Rome was founded and welcomed Aeneas.
iphitas: Named for Iphitus, whose bow Odysseus carried and used to slay the suitors.
phorbanta: Named for Phorbas, a hero of several Greek tales, among them the boxer who challenged travellers to Delphi.
peranthus: Named for Peranthus; Fabricius's coinage, apparently from the Greek for around the flowers.
delalandii: Named for Pierre Antoine Delalande, the Paris museum's collector at the Cape of Good Hope, who died in 1823.
agapenor: Named for Agapenor, leader of the Arcadians at Troy, whose ships were blown to Cyprus on the way home.
pompilius: Named for Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome and founder of its religious calendar.
dissimilis: Dissimilis means unlike in Latin: Linnaeus named the mime for looking nothing like its relatives.
celestina: Celestina means heavenly, for the frosted blue of the wings.
lycimnia: Named for Licymnius, the uncle of Heracles.
ada: Named for Ada, the Carian queen who adopted Alexander the Great as her son.
eriphia: Named for Eriphia, one of the nymphs who nursed the infant Dionysus.
isse: Named for Isse, daughter of Macareus, loved by Apollo in the guise of a shepherd.
epicharis: Named for Epicharis, the freedwoman who kept silent under torture during the conspiracy against Nero.
endeis: Named for Endeis, mother of Peleus and grandmother of Achilles.
eupompe: Eupompe means fair procession in Greek, the name of a Nereid.
achine: Named for Achine; Cramer's spelling of a name of uncertain origin.
evarne: Named for Evarne, one of the Nereids.
proterpia: Named for Proterpia; Fabricius's coinage from the Greek for delighting first.
smilax: Named for Smilax, the nymph who loved the youth Crocus and was turned into the bindweed that bears her name.
gnidus: Named for Cnidus, the Greek city of Asia Minor famous for its statue of Aphrodite.
lysippus: Named for Lysippus, the sculptor of Alexander the Great.
phareus: Named for Pharos, the island lighthouse of Alexandria.
jafra: Named for Jaffa, the ancient port of Palestine.
longinus: Named for Longinus, the Greek critic to whom the treatise On the Sublime is attributed.
helus: Named for Helos, a town of Laconia whose people became the helots of Sparta.
eunice: Named for Eunice, one of the Nereids.
midama: Named by Linnaeus for Midamus; the name is his own coinage.
niavia: Named for Niavius; Linnaeus's coinage, of uncertain meaning.
agelia: Named for Agelaus, a Greek name meaning leader of the people.
zidora: Named for Zidora, of uncertain origin; Cramer had earlier called this butterfly Egina.
euryta: Named by Linnaeus for Eurytus, a king of Oechalia and famous archer.
narcea: Named for Narcaea, an epithet of Athena at Olympia.
aglatonice: Named for Aglaonice, the Thessalian woman said to be the first female astronomer in Greece.
cloantha: Named for Cloanthus, one of Aeneas's captains in the Aeneid.
orthosia: Orthosia is an epithet of Artemis, the upright one.
larinia: Named for Larinum, an ancient town of Italy.
thadana: Named for Thadana; Cramer had earlier called this butterfly Hyperia.
mycerina: Named for Mycerinus, the Greek form of Menkaure, builder of the third pyramid at Giza.
iphicla: Named for Iphiclus, the swift-footed son of Phylacus, an Argonaut.
iapis: Named for Iapis, the physician who healed Aeneas's wound in the Aeneid.
hydarnis: Named for Hydarnes, a Persian general of Xerxes who commanded the Immortals at Thermopylae.
anthiocus: Named for Antiochus, the name of the Seleucid kings of Syria.
condomanus: Named for Condomanus; Fabricius's coinage of uncertain origin.
lasinassa: Named for Lasinassa; Fabricius's coinage, one of a dozen names this variable species has borne.
nephalion: Named for Nephalion, a son of Minos killed by Heracles at Paros.
dimas: Named for Dymas, king of Phrygia and father of Hecuba.
lysithous: Named for Lysithous; Fabricius's coinage, of uncertain origin.
licoraeus: Named for Lycoreus, a son of Apollo and founder of Lycoreia on Parnassus.
polymetus: Named for Polymetus; Cramer's coinage, from the Greek for much counsel.
erecteus: Named for Erechtheus, the legendary king of Athens whose temple stands on the Acropolis.
thyria: Named for Thyria, a town of Elis in Greece.
pitys: Named for Pitys, the nymph pursued by Pan and turned into a pine tree.
virginia: Named for Virginia, the colony, or for the Roman maiden of that name; the species is American.
coronea: Named for Coronea, the town of Boeotia where the Spartans fought in 394 BC.
oenippe: Named for Oenippe; Fabricius's coinage from the Greek for wine-horse.
